clue.text: 'Fish', 'good', 'bash' — one of those four-letter words

parts.note: a tetra is the small bright fish of home aquariums
g is the standard abbreviation for good, as on a school report
to bash into something is to ram it

explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks are the instruction: each of the three words is being handed over as material rather than read for sense, and each of them really is four letters long.
explanation.definitionFit: A tetragram is any group of four letters, so every quoted example qualifies as one — Greek tetra- simply counts them.

clue.text: Runner in European capital concerned with section going uphill

indicators.note: This is a down entry, so a piece sent uphill arrives with its letters read from the foot of the grid upwards.

parts.note: re is the heading on a memo, meaning concerning
a bit of something is a section of it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Runner' is the crossword's standing word for a river, and the capital it runs through is Rome — neither is named, so the definition passes for an athlete abroad.
explanation.definitionFit: Runner in European capital → TIBER: rivers run, and this is the river Rome was built on, so the phrase locates it rather than naming it.

clue.text: Bad speller in theory, extremely anxious

indicators.note: 'In theory' passes for an idiom while doing literal work: what stands before it drops inside what comes after.
The extremes of a word are its two ends, so only the outermost letters are kept.

parts.note: the two ends of THEORY, its first and last letters, with the middle discarded
not somebody who misspells words but somebody who casts them, and wickedly

explanation.walkthrough: The joke is 'bad speller', which reads as a hopeless orthographer and means a caster of evil spells. Everything else in the sentence is machinery dressed as small talk.
explanation.definitionFit: anxious → TWITCHY: a twitchy person cannot keep still for nerves, so the word names the visible fidgeting instead of the feeling behind it.

clue.text: Long speech finally wrapped up by wizard

indicators.note: It points at the end of the word, so the letter that finishes it is the only one taken.

parts.note: an ace is a wizard at something — the expert, not the conjuror — and the word opens after its second letter

indicators.note: Anything wrapped up has a covering closed round it, so the piece named next goes outside.

parts.note: the closing letter of speecH

explanation.walkthrough: 'Long' opens the clue looking like an adjective sizing up the speech, and it is really the verb — to long for something.
explanation.definitionFit: Long → ACHE: to ache for a thing is to yearn for it, and both verbs carry the sense of a want that hurts.

clue.text: Red colour a revolutionary adopts

indicators.note: What a phrase adopts it takes in and keeps, so the letters are already sitting inside these words.

parts.note: four letters in a row bridge the end of the first word, the whole of the second and the start of the third

explanation.walkthrough: A colour and a revolutionary side by side look like two pieces of wordplay to solve, when the phrase is only a hiding place. 'Red' here is the steak, not the politics.
explanation.definitionFit: Red → RARE: a steak served red in the middle is a rare one, which is the kitchen's plain term for that degree of cooking.

clue.text: Noted progression without cabbage being mentioned?

indicators.note: To mention a thing is to say it, so what counts is the sound of the words and not their spelling.

parts.note: without means minus, and said aloud its closing S runs on into the next word instead of staying put
the cabbage meant is kale, and it collects the S that the word before let go

explanation.walkthrough: The whole trick is where one word stops and the next starts: the sound never changes, only the gap moves. Say the two greengrocery words quickly and the music appears.
explanation.definitionFit: Noted progression → MINOR SCALE: a scale is a ladder of notes climbing in order, and the minor pattern is the sadder-sounding of the two standard ones.

clue.text: Man, say, placing one page between the sheets?

indicators.note: It is an instruction about position rather than meaning — something is being put somewhere.
Between fixes that position exactly: the letters go in the middle of the word, not in front of it or after it.

parts.note: to be between the sheets is to be in bed, and the word opens after its first letter
the Roman numeral for one
p is the usual abbreviation for page

explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' is the marker that the definition is only an example: a man is one kind of two-legged creature and far from the only one. The surface suggests something else entirely.
explanation.definitionFit: Man, say → BIPED: humans walk on two legs, so 'man' is offered as one instance of the class rather than as a synonym for it.

clue.text: Very anxious when building house?

definitions.meaning: the slang phrase for being frightened out of your wits
read literally, laying the courses that make the walls

explanation.walkthrough: The second reading is a joke rather than a dictionary sense, which is what the question mark concedes: a builder halfway up a wall is doing this in the innocent way.
explanation.definitionFit: Very anxious → BRICKING IT is British slang for terrified; the other reading takes the same words literally, as laying bricks.

clue.text: Keen I observe, nothing to lose in school

indicators.note: What is lost has gone from the word, so the letter named just before it drops out.
It marks the insertion: everything assembled so far goes inside the word that follows.

parts.note: a school of whales is a pod, and it opens between its second and third letters
the pronoun taken exactly as it stands, one letter
to observe is to note, and 'nothing' is the O that goes

explanation.walkthrough: 'Nothing to lose' reads as a gambler's shrug and is really naming the letter O. The school is a gathering of whales, not a building full of children.
explanation.definitionFit: Keen → POINTED: a keen blade and a pointed one are both sharp, and both words transfer to a remark meant to cut.

clue.text: Pattern has Dorothy frolicking in spring, did you say?

parts.note: Dot is the familiar short form of Dorothy

indicators.note: It asks you to trust your ear: the words in front of it are to be heard rather than spelled.

parts.note: frolics are tricks and the spring month is May, and the two run together into one word when spoken

explanation.walkthrough: A dot matrix printer builds every character out of a grid of dots, which is the pattern meant — and Dorothy's nickname is a dot in its own right.
explanation.definitionFit: Pattern → DOT MATRIX: the grid of dots a printer or a display uses to form characters, so it is a pattern made of dots by definition.

clue.text: Muppet Amin confined to more cheerful block?

parts.note: blithe means cheerful, and the comparative just adds an R

indicators.note: Somebody confined is shut inside somewhere, so the name goes within the words that follow rather than beside them.

parts.note: an ingot is a block of cast metal, and it opens after its first three letters
Idi Amin, the Ugandan dictator, hands over his first name

explanation.walkthrough: 'Muppet' is playground slang for a fool, which the question mark quietly concedes. Amin's forename is the crossword's usual way of getting three awkward letters into a grid.
explanation.definitionFit: Muppet → BLITHERING IDIOT: British slang calls a fool a muppet, after the puppets, and this is the same insult said at full length.

clue.text: Brilliant music?

definitions.meaning: a brilliant is a diamond cut to fifty-eight facets, and the trade's slang for a big stone is this
the loud guitar-and-drums kind, named for the way it rolls

explanation.walkthrough: Two words and two definitions, with nothing between them to say which is which — the question mark is the only sign that 'brilliant' is a noun here rather than praise.
explanation.definitionFit: Brilliant → ROCK is the jeweller's slang for a big cut diamond; music → ROCK is the guitar-driven genre, two senses that share nothing but a spelling.

clue.text: Old banger taking the biscuit with breakdown truck, would you say?

indicators.note: It hands the clue to the ear: what matters is how the two phrases sound run together, not how they are written down.

parts.note: the biscuit is a cracker, and said aloud its opening is spelled quite differently
a breakdown truck tows, so it is a tower, and the sound runs straight on from the piece before

explanation.walkthrough: 'Old banger' is a wreck of a car on the surface and something that banged in 1883 underneath: the eruption was heard thousands of miles away across the Indian Ocean.
explanation.definitionFit: Old banger → KRAKATOA: the volcano's 1883 eruption is the loudest bang in recorded history, so the scrapyard phrase for a clapped-out car doubles as a joke.

clue.text: Plain character gets surly, I gathered

indicators.note: Things gathered are swept together into a heap, and letters in a heap no longer lie in the order they arrived in.

parts.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a small domestic sulk, and 'I gathered' passes for 'so I understood' while doing the shuffling. Plain here is the opposite of beautiful, not of fancy.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain character → UGLY SISTER: Cinderella's two sisters are the pantomime's stock plain ones, so 'character' points at a role in a story.

clue.text: Photo briefly capturing mother, teacher and a princess

indicators.note: A word given briefly is given short, so its final letter never gets written down.
A camera captures whatever it shuts inside the frame, and here the words that follow are held within the piece before them.

parts.note: a photo is a print, docked of its last letter; what is left opens up before its own final N
ma is the nursery word for mother
a don is a university teacher
the word a, taken as it stands, landing at the very end

explanation.walkthrough: 'Capturing' does double duty as what a camera does and as the instruction to hold something inside. The print is the darkroom kind, not the newspaper kind.
explanation.definitionFit: princess → PRIMA DONNA: both are everyday names for somebody who expects to be indulged, the opera sense of leading lady having soured into temperament.

clue.text: Dash a cigar off that's poisonous

definitions.note: The answer is a mushroom, a noun, while 'poisonous' is an adjective; the setter's 'that's' does the joining, so the definition reads as 'the thing that is poisonous'.

parts.note: to fly somewhere is to dash there

indicators.note: Food that has gone off has turned, and turned letters no longer sit in the order they were served in.

parts.note: anagram fodder, six letters

explanation.walkthrough: 'Dash a cigar off' reads as one impatient gesture, which is exactly what hides the join between the two pieces. The toadstool meant is the storybook one: scarlet cap, white spots.
explanation.definitionFit: poisonous → FLY AGARIC: the red-and-white toadstool is genuinely toxic, and it is named for the old practice of using it to kill flies.

clue.text: Miss payment claiming one pocketed by singers

indicators.note: To claim a thing is to take it to yourself, so the singers take the letter inside them.

parts.note: a fee is a payment, and it splits after its first letter

indicators.note: What is pocketed goes into somebody's pocket and out of sight, so the whole group lands within the payment.

parts.note: altos are the singers between the sopranos and the tenors
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.walkthrough: Two insertions nested one inside the other, and the surface never stops sounding like a dispute over an invoice. Only 'Miss' stands outside the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Miss → FAIL TO SEE: to miss a thing is to fail to notice it, and the phrase is what English says when a point has gone straight past somebody.

clue.text: Some villain, a director, the lowest of the low

indicators.note: 'Some' asks for a part rather than the whole, and the part wanted is a run of letters lying end to end.

parts.note: five letters in a row run from the tail of the first word, through the second and into the third

explanation.walkthrough: The comma after 'villain' is the disguise: it makes two separate people out of what is really one unbroken run of letters in a film-set sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: the lowest of the low → NADIR: astronomy's nadir is the point directly beneath your feet, opposite the zenith, and English borrows it for any rock bottom.

clue.text: Irritable and hot in Windy City

indicators.note: A windy day blows things out of place, and letters blown about do not come down in the order they went up.
It puts the single letter among the ones being shuffled rather than beside them.

parts.note: h is the letter on the hot tap
anagram fodder, four letters

explanation.walkthrough: 'Windy City' is Chicago and has nothing to do with the answer: the two words have to be prised apart, one as the instruction and one as the material.
explanation.definitionFit: Irritable → ITCHY: an itch makes you fidget and snap, and the word has long carried that figurative sense of restless impatience.

clue.text: Actress and singer also going up in smoke

parts.note: Cher has an Oscar and a shelf of hit records, so she answers to both descriptions

indicators.note: This is a down entry, so a word going up the grid is read from its foot to its head.

parts.note: also means too, and this is that word before it is turned

explanation.walkthrough: 'Going up in smoke' is one idiom on the surface and two separate instructions underneath. The turn stops short of 'in', which is doing nothing but joining.
explanation.definitionFit: smoke → CHEROOT: a cheroot is a cigar cut square at both ends, and 'a smoke' is the everyday noun for anything you light and draw on.

clue.text: Consider framing suggestion with old pictures

definitions.note: 'Pictures' is plural and the answer is a single building; 'the pictures' has been the collective English name for the cinema since the silent era, so the plural names one place.

indicators.note: A frame goes round whatever it holds, so the word before it closes around the piece named next.

parts.note: to mull a thing over is to consider it, and the word opens before its last letter
a tip is a helpful suggestion
ex- is the prefix for a former anything

explanation.walkthrough: 'Old pictures' reads as a run of classic films, and that is where the definition hides: only 'pictures' belongs to it, while 'old' is two more letters of wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: pictures → MULTIPLEX: going to the pictures means going to the cinema, and a multiplex is the cinema with a dozen screens under one roof.

clue.text: One defined by 'scummy fellow'?

indicators.note: Scum is filth that has risen out of place, so whatever the word describes is not sitting the way it should.

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one, which the rest is built around
anagram fodder, six letters

explanation.walkthrough: Every word works twice: read straight the sentence says what the answer means, and read again it is the recipe for building it. The quotation marks flag the phrase as material.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue is the definition: a lowlife is exactly the sort of person the quoted phrase picks out, a contemptible specimen.

clue.text: Intervals including notes a perfect fifth apart horrifying singers?

indicators.note: To include a thing is to take it in, so the pieces named next sit inside the word before them.

parts.note: a third is a musical interval, and the word opens after its second letter
count E up to B and you cover five steps of the scale, the interval called a perfect fifth

explanation.walkthrough: The clue is all music until the last two words, when it turns into Hitchcock. Even the definition keeps up the pretence, since birds sing and 'singers' still sounds musical.
explanation.definitionFit: horrifying singers? → THE BIRDS: Hitchcock's film turns ordinary songbirds into a murderous flock, and the question mark admits this is a description rather than a synonym.

clue.text: Kiss and Wham on tour?

indicators.note: A band on tour is never in the same place two nights running, and neither are these letters.

parts.note: anagram fodder — the eighties pop duo, four letters

explanation.walkthrough: Kiss and Wham are both bands, which is the joke: only one of them is being used as a band, and the other is quietly the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Kiss → MWAH: mwah is the written-down noise of an air kiss, so the sound stands in for the act it accompanies.

clue.text: Growly dog

definitions.meaning: of a voice that comes out low and rough, as after a night of shouting
the thick-coated sled breed of the Arctic

explanation.walkthrough: Two words, and each of them is a complete definition — there is no wordplay to find at all, which is how the clue can afford to be this short.
explanation.definitionFit: A husky voice is hoarse and low, while a husky is the Arctic sled breed — two senses that share a spelling and nothing else.

clue.text: Stumpy tail — 's pruned

parts.note: the letter is handed over on its own, inside quotation marks
a pruned branch is one that has been cut

explanation.walkthrough: The dash does all the disguising: it turns a definition and two scraps of wordplay into what looks like a single passing remark about an animal.
explanation.definitionFit: Stumpy tail → SCUT: a scut is the short erect tail of a rabbit, hare or deer, the countryman's word for exactly that stub.

clue.text: Test of popular opinion to the north

indicators.note: A test OF something takes its material out of that thing, and the setter leans on the little word lightly — it is all the notice you get that the letters are already there.
This is a down entry, so letters travelling north are read from the bottom of the grid upwards.

parts.note: four letters in a row straddle the gap between these two words, and the entry climbs back up through them

explanation.walkthrough: A test of popular opinion is a poll, which is the answer the surface is offering and not the one wanted. Nothing has been rearranged here, only read the other way.
explanation.definitionFit: Test → ORAL: an oral is the spoken examination — a language viva, say — so 'test' names it by what it is rather than by how it is conducted.

clue.text: One's disempowered when had by those, Spooner's Margaret, Temple and MacLaine?

definitions.text: One's disempowered when had by those

indicators.note: The Reverend Spooner traded the opening sounds of two words, so his name alone is the instruction to swap them over.

parts.note: Margaret Court won more grand slam titles than anyone; she hands her C over and takes SH in exchange
the joining word between the names stays exactly where it stands
Shirley Temple and Shirley MacLaine make a pair of Shirleys, and they collect the C the tennis player gave up

explanation.walkthrough: Say the plain version first — a tennis champion and two actresses — and Spooner does the rest. What comes out is an idiom with nothing to do with any of them.
explanation.definitionFit: Having somebody by the short and curlies means having them at your mercy; the phrase names body hair whose grip leaves no room to argue.

clue.text: Hog radiator, say, when first cut off

indicators.note: The first of anything is its opening letter, and cut off means that letter does not survive into the grid.

parts.note: a radiator is one kind of heater, which is what 'say' is marking, and this is the word before its front letter goes

explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' is doing the work of a definition-by-example in the wordplay rather than the definition: the clue needs the general word first, and only then docks a letter from it.
explanation.definitionFit: Hog → EATER: to hog food is to take it all, and a hog is a glutton, so the word names somebody by appetite rather than by species.

clue.text: Arsenal's feeble passing through channel

indicators.note: Whatever passes through a channel is inside it for the length of the journey, so these letters sit within the word that follows.

parts.note: an artery is the channel blood travels down, and it opens after its third letter
somebody feeble is ill, weak from sickness

explanation.walkthrough: Arsenal are the Gunners, which is the joke the capital letter is trying to sell you. The arsenal wanted is the older sense: a store of weapons.
explanation.definitionFit: Arsenal → ARTILLERY: an arsenal is a stock of weaponry, and artillery is the heavy-gun branch of it, so both words name the hardware collectively.
